sections.h2: What an Ohio transfer on death designation affidavit is
sections.html:
It is a sworn document naming who gets an Ohio home or other real estate when the owner dies, with no probate transfer of that parcel. The authority is Revised Code 5302.22, with companion rules in sections 5302.222 and 5302.23.

The affidavit works only if it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death. No buyer's signature is needed, no payment, and no delivery to the person named. Ohio law also treats a transfer made this way as not testamentary, so for that property it outranks a will or the intestacy rules.

Some owners confuse this with a transfer on death deed. Ohio's current statute calls the instrument an affidavit. The older deed form survives only for designations made before the 2009 change.

sections.h2: Who can sign and what goes in the affidavit
sections.html:
Sole owners, tenants in common and survivorship tenants may sign, and a married owner signs jointly with the spouse. The designation can cover the whole interest or a stated fraction.

Someone authorized to administer oaths must verify the signing. Division (D) of section 5302.22 calls for these items:

  • A legal description of the land, with a pointer to a recorded instrument that contains it.
  • A statement of the exact part being passed, if it is less than everything.
  • The signer's statement that the record shows the signer as owner at the time of recording, along with marital status.
  • For a married signer, the spouse's statement that dower rights give way to the beneficiary's title.
  • One or more beneficiaries, each named individually.

A knowingly false statement is falsification under division (A)(6) of section 2921.13. Recorders do not draft documents, so most owners hire an attorney or use a title company.

sections.h2: Recording the affidavit and the cost
sections.html:
The owner brings it to the recorder in the county where the land sits. The recorder files it the way a deed is filed, charges the deed fee, and indexes it under the signing owner's name.

Section 317.32 splits each charge into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. A county may also add a document preservation surcharge capped at $5, so the final bill varies by county. Ask the recorder for the all-in number before you send a check.

Local practice can add a step. In Pickaway County, a transfer on death designation cannot be mailed in, because it needs auditor and engineer stamps first and must be carried to the office.

sections.h2: Ownership while the owner is alive
sections.html:
Nothing changes. Section 5302.23 gives the designation no effect on present ownership, and the named beneficiary holds no interest until the owner dies. The owner can still sell, mortgage, lease or live in the house.

For a seller this means a buyer's title company will see the recorded affidavit in the chain of title, but you can convey by deed without the beneficiary's consent. When a deed to a buyer is recorded, the affidavit has nothing left to act on.

Lienholders are unaffected as well. A mortgagee, judgment creditor or mechanic's lien holder keeps every right it had, and it need not name the beneficiary in a foreclosure unless that person holds some other interest in the land.

An owner can do it at any time without the beneficiary's consent. Record a new transfer on death designation affidavit stating the change, and the later-recorded one supersedes every earlier recorded affidavit for that property.

The statute also builds in several automatic effects:

  • If a named beneficiary dies first and a contingent beneficiary was named, the contingent person takes the same share.
  • If no named beneficiary survives and none is contingent, the interest falls into the owner's probate estate.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal shares as tenants in common unless the affidavit says otherwise or makes them survivorship tenants.
  • If the owner's spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, the spouse is treated as having died before the owner.

A recorded affidavit also keeps dower rights from vesting in a spouse the owner marries afterward, unless the designation is changed or revoked.

sections.h2: What the beneficiary files after the owner dies
sections.html:
The beneficiary signs an affidavit of confirmation. Under Section 5302.222, the beneficiary presents it to the auditor of the county where the land lies and then files it with that county's recorder. A notary or other oath-giver verifies it, and a certified copy of the death certificate goes with it.

The statute fixes its contents: each surviving beneficiary's name and address, the date the owner died, the property description, and the names of any beneficiaries who did not survive. For each one who died first, a certified death certificate is attached too.

Land under the Chapter 5309 registration system follows a separate route in section 5309.081. In every case the beneficiary receives only what the owner held at death, along with each mortgage, reservation or exception already tied to the land.

sections.h2: Conveyance fee on a transfer on death
sections.html:
Often there is none, though the auditor makes the call. The list in section 319.54(G)(3) exempts, among others, a transfer where no money or other valuable and tangible consideration changes hands and that is not a gift. For an exempt transfer, section 319.202 asks only for a statement of the reason.

The form family is DTE 100. In Paulding County the auditor uses DTE 100 (EX) to claim an exemption, while Pickaway County will not transfer anything without a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX. Check with your own auditor before filing an affidavit of confirmation.

Recording is billed separately from anything the auditor takes, at the same rate as a deed.

sections.h2: Selling a house with a recorded affidavit
sections.html:
It can be sold. While the owner lives, the owner signs a deed and closing goes ahead as usual. After the owner has died, the beneficiary must record the affidavit of confirmation before a deed to any buyer will clear the auditor and the recorder.

Skipping an estate for this parcel can save weeks. The beneficiary still carries the mortgage balance, any back property tax, needed repairs and co-owners, because the property arrives burdened by whatever is on record.

An heir who wants to sell an Ohio house as-is for cash should expect the buyer to ask for the recorded affidavit of confirmation first.

faqs.q: Does a transfer on death affidavit keep a house out of probate in Ohio?
faqs.a: For the covered parcel, yes. Section 5302.23 makes the transfer non-testamentary and overrides a will or an intestate transfer of that property. A parcel with no surviving named or contingent beneficiary lands in the probate estate.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to sign?
faqs.a: No. Under 5302.22(F) the affidavit needs no payment and no delivery to the beneficiary. It takes effect once recorded with the county recorder during the owner's life.

faqs.q: May an owner name a trust as the beneficiary?
faqs.a: Yes. A beneficiary may be a natural or legal person, such as a bank serving as trustee. If a successor trustee replaces the named trustee before the owner dies, the successor stands in, and the affidavit of confirmation lists that successor.

faqs.q: What happens if the owner was married when signing?
faqs.a: The spouse signs too, and the spouse's dower rights give way to the beneficiary's title. If the spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, that designation ends.

faqs.q: Can a lender still foreclose on a house with a recorded affidavit?
faqs.a: Yes. Lienholders keep every right, and the beneficiary inherits subject to existing encumbrances. A lender suing to foreclose need not name the beneficiary unless that person has some other interest in the land.
